item.title: Tuta encrypted email and its Nextcloud integration
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Tuta and Nextcloud launched an integration on 1 October that lets you use Tuta inside Nextcloud, save received attachments to Nextcloud and create Nextcloud Talk meeting links from Tuta Calendar. A Nextcloud administrator has to install the app, and as of 18 October neither announcement explains how attachments are protected once they are in Nextcloud.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Tuta, Nextcloud, CyberInsider

Encrypted email service Tuta and the open-source collaboration platform Nextcloud launched an integration on 1 October, which Tuta's announcement describes as free. It has two parts: a Tuta Mail app in the Nextcloud App Store that runs Tuta's web client inside Nextcloud, and a Nextcloud plugin in Tuta that saves received attachments to Nextcloud with one click or creates a Nextcloud Talk meeting link when you set up a Tuta Calendar event. Both features need the Tuta Mail app on your own Nextcloud; the App Store page lists Nextcloud 33 to 35. On a self-hosted server the administrator installs it, and on a managed one the provider has to make it available.

According to Tuta's announcement, the account administrator enables the plugin for all users under Settings → Plugins, and a single user is their own administrator. Tuta's README on GitHub lists two settings, the Nextcloud address and the folder for attachments, and the features work inside Nextcloud as well as in Tuta's web, desktop and mobile clients. Per Nextcloud's press release, the integration makes it easier for individuals and small businesses to self-host Nextcloud while leaving email to Tuta.

As of 18 October, neither Tuta's announcement nor its pricing page says which plan is required. Tuta's apps have a Traditional Chinese interface. In Tuta's public source code as of 18 October, the Traditional Chinese language file covers the general Plugins page, while the Nextcloud plugin's own settings and buttons such as "Save to Nextcloud" exist only in English and German.

Perspective

Tuta's encryption page says emails, including subject lines and all attachments, are end-to-end encrypted and the key is never shared with anyone, Tuta included. Neither announcement explains what happens to that protection once an attachment is saved to Nextcloud, so we read Tuta's public source code as of 18 October. The save button sits in the attachment-saving dialog, and the plugin uploads through Nextcloud's file access interface (WebDAV) without any extra encryption. Our inference is that the uploaded file is the decrypted one, and it leaves Tuta's end-to-end encryption when it reaches Nextcloud.

Nextcloud's administration manual distinguishes two kinds of encryption. Server-side encryption runs on the server with keys stored there, and the manual warns that it does not protect against a compromised server or a malicious administrator. End-to-end encryption is done by Nextcloud's desktop or mobile clients before upload. Because the plugin does not upload through those clients, how well an attachment is protected on Nextcloud depends on that server's settings and who runs it, which is our inference from the manual and the code.

For Talk, the source code shows the plugin creating a public conversation, which Talk's API documentation lists as one that allows guests. Nextcloud's product page says Talk supports end-to-end encrypted calls in the web and new desktop clients, without saying whether public conversations are covered.

In mainland China, the third-party monitor GreatFire rates tuta.com as intermittently disrupted, with 59% of the last 17 conclusive tests up to 11 October showing interference. In India, the Internet Freedom Foundation noted reports that 14 end-to-end encrypted and peer-to-peer messaging apps, not email services, were banned in May 2023 without a published order. In April 2025 the Karnataka High Court ordered central authorities to act to block Proton Mail, though MediaNama noted that Proton Mail was still reachable in India when it reported the order. We found no reports of Tuta itself being blocked in India.

People or teams already using Nextcloud and Tuta can have the Nextcloud administrator install the Tuta Mail app, then have the Tuta account administrator enable the plugin. The manual notes that server-side encryption does not protect against the server's administrators, so before saving sensitive attachments it is worth checking who has administrative access to that server. Based on the source code and Talk's documentation, the plugin creates public conversations that allow guests, so anyone with the link can join as a guest.

item.title: Signal's cross-platform encrypted backups and password manager transfers on Android
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Signal released iOS 8.30 on 28 September, and its encrypted Signal Secure Backups can now be restored between Android and iPhone, so chats can follow you to a new platform. In September Google added a way on Android to move passwords and passkeys between password managers without exporting a file, starting with four apps.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 21 sources, including Signal, Google, Android Developers

Signal released iOS 8.30 on 28 September, and according to its blog, encrypted backups can now be created and restored across Android, iOS and desktop. The support centre limits this to Signal Secure Backups, which can be restored between Android and iPhone, so chat history can move to a new platform when you change phones. On 10 September Google added a flow on Android for moving passwords and passkeys from one password manager to another without first downloading them to a file. It works on Android 8 and later, and the announcement lists Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden and Dashlane, with more partners to follow.

According to the support centre, Signal Secure Backups is hosted by Signal and protected by a 64-character recovery key that is never shared with the Signal service. If the key is lost, the backup cannot be restored, and Signal cannot recover it. As of 18 October the free plan backs up all text messages and the last 45 days of media, while a US$1.99 monthly plan stores up to 100 GB of media. View-once messages and messages set to disappear within 24 hours are left out.

Per Signal's blog, a new hosted backup is created every 24 hours and the previous one is deleted. The troubleshooting page notes that a backup can only be restored during first-time setup, using the same phone number.

If both phones are at hand and on the same platform, a device-to-device transfer moves the chat history to the new phone and leaves nothing on the old one. In iOS 8.30, Signal uses Wi-Fi Aware to set up a local end-to-end encrypted link between two iPhones, which the blog credits with better speed and reliability.

On-device backup files, according to the blog, can be created on Android, iOS and desktop in a cross-platform format. As of 18 October the support centre pages describe this differently from the blog and from each other: a page updated on 11 October lists all three platforms but restores work only within the same platform, while a troubleshooting page updated on 3 October limits them to Android to Android. Both the backups and transfers page and the desktop backups page note that an Android or desktop backup file cannot be restored on an iPhone.

In Google's announcement, the move starts in the new password manager, where you choose to import from another provider. Android then lists the password managers on the phone that can export, and you select, review and authorise the transfer in the old one. According to Google's developer documentation, the transfer happens between two apps on the same device without exposing raw credentials to the Android OS or unauthenticated apps. It uses the FIDO Alliance's Credential Exchange Format (CXF) and covers passwords, passkeys, addresses and custom fields; the FIDO Alliance is the industry group behind passkeys and other sign-in standards.

Apple offers developers of password managers a similar export and import API from iOS 26 and macOS 26, and in the flow its documentation describes, the operating system confirms the identities of both apps and writes nothing to the file system. A WWDC25 developer session notes that the data format was built with members of the FIDO Alliance. As of 18 October, the export and import pages of Apple's iPhone User Guide still cover only CSV files, and the export page warns that exported passwords are not encrypted.

Perspective

Signal backups are encrypted with the user's recovery key, and without it no one, including Signal, can read or restore a backup. iCloud backups do not carry Signal chats either; the support centre's FAQ lists them as not compatible with Signal.

Signal Secure Backups adds a supplemental key that rotates daily and is kept in a trusted execution environment (TEE, an isolated area of a processor) on Signal's hosted service. This key cannot decrypt a backup without the recovery key, and the blog describes its sole purpose as forward secrecy, meaning past data stays protected even if a key leaks later. On-device backups cannot use the same TEE to get forward secrecy. The blog calls a TEE the best current way to protect this key, though that may change as research continues.

According to Google's announcement, moving passwords used to mean downloading them into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys could not be moved at all. On Apple's side, the new transfer writes nothing to the file system. On Android, the two apps pass data through a secure content URI backed by temporary cache files. The documentation's reason is that a whole vault can exceed Android's 1MB limit for a single transaction between processes.

According to heise, whether a whole vault can move depends on whether both apps have implemented the standard. Google's help page explains that importing into Google Password Manager requires signing in to the other password manager, and importing passkeys may also prompt for a recovery key. The page also reminds users to make sure they trust the other password manager before importing.

In parts of Asia, changing phones also involves a government ID stored on the phone. Japan's Digital Agency, on its machine-translated English page last updated on 25 August, advises users to delete the My Number Card from a smartphone before giving it up or changing models. For electronic certificates on Android phones, the law obliges users to revoke them themselves, and initialising the phone does not delete them.

In South Korea, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety's mobile ID site, available only in Korean, explains that a mobile resident registration card must be reissued after changing phones. Holders of IC cards can tap the card on the new phone and verify their identity, while holders of older cards can apply for an IC card or visit a community centre and complete the reissue with a QR code at the counter. Korea.net, the government portal, reported in March 2025 that each person can have a mobile ID on only one smartphone.

In mainland China, the third-party monitor GreatFire found both signal.org and play.google.com fully blocked in tests up to 11 October. GreatFire measures whether websites can be reached, not whether the Signal app can send messages. In Android's developer documentation, the caller check for this transfer flow is tied to the Google Play services system component, with nothing on whether phones without Google Play services can use it.

Signal users planning to switch phones can turn on backups in Signal's settings on the old phone and keep the recovery key safe before switching. The key can be saved to a password manager or stored manually; if it goes into a password manager, you will need to be able to open that manager on the new phone or another device, which is our inference from the setup flow. Signal Secure Backups covers a lost phone or a platform change, but cannot be restored with a new phone number, and the blog reminds users never to share the recovery key.

To switch password managers on Android, open the new app and look for an import option, and both apps need to support the flow. Google's 10 September announcement lists Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden and Dashlane. Importing into Google Password Manager also requires verifying your identity with the phone's screen lock. iPhone users moving passwords through a CSV file should note Apple's warning that the exported file is not encrypted and anyone who can access it can read it.

item.title: Weekly brief, 2026 week 42
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Seven stories from 3 to 11 October: a now-patched file-reading flaw in Telegram Desktop, Bitwarden's app store builds moving to a commercial licence, LineageOS 24 based on Android 17, Nitter seeking funding and legal help, a DNS ad blocker built on an ESP32-C3, a mobile internet shutdown and a platform advisory in New Delhi, and Psiphon weighing a move out of Canada over Bill C-22.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including beaksec, GitHub, Bitwarden Community Forums

This issue collects seven stories from 3 to 11 October.

File-reading flaw in Telegram Desktop

A researcher disclosed on 3 October a flaw in Telegram Desktop 7.2.8 and earlier: a single click on a crafted link outside Telegram could send local files to an attacker. The files could include login data that let the attacker take over the account, and the researcher confirmed it only on Windows. The researcher writes that a Telegram commit on GitHub on 16 September fixed the problem and that 7.2.9, released on 17 September, includes the fix, though the official release notes mention only an unrelated rendering fix.

Telegram Desktop users can check that they are on 7.2.9 or later. The researcher also suggests setting a local passcode, while noting that it only makes stolen login data unusable and does not stop files from being read.

Bitwarden's store builds move to a commercial licence

A Bitwarden staff member announced on the community forum on 9 October that, starting with the next release, the apps published in app stores will be the commercially licensed builds. In replies, staff added that direct downloads from the website will also be commercially licensed. The announcement says the GPLv3 open-source version will continue to be updated and published on GitHub and that all current features are in both versions, but a staff reply also says some future components will be published under the commercial licence and exist only in that build.

Another staff member wrote on the forum that the change only affects those repackaging and reselling Bitwarden and that self-hosting is unaffected. As of 12 October, the licence file on GitHub was last changed in 2025. It still covers GPLv3 plus the Bitwarden License, which applies only to the bitwarden_license directory, and we could not find the commercial build's licence text on the website.

LineageOS 24

LineageOS, an operating system built on Android's open-source code that users can install on their own phones, announced version 24.0, based on Android 17, on its official blog on 11 October. It launches for a selection of devices, with more added as they meet the project's requirements. For devices on Linux kernels 4.4 and 4.9, the project only accepts 22.2 builds, which the blog says will keep receiving monthly security patches until Google stops publishing official security bulletins for Android 15.

Users already on an official build can follow their device's upgrade guide and do not need to wipe their device unless its wiki page says otherwise.

Nitter seeks funding and legal help

According to its README, Nitter is a free and open-source alternative front end for X (Twitter) focused on privacy. Its maintainer posted on nitter.net on 10 October that X Corp. sent cease-and-desist letters on 24 August and 8 September demanding a permanent takedown of Nitter instances and the project's repository. The post says the maintainer's 7 September update about having legal representation relied on assurances that turned out to be untrue. As of the 10 October post, Nitter has no legal counsel, and the maintainer is seeking funding and legal help.

TechCrunch reported in August that the letter accused Nitter of unlawful use and circumvention of X's API. As of 12 October, nitter.net shows only the announcement.

A DNS ad blocker built on an ESP32-C3

The open-source GitHub project esp32-c3-adblock puts Pi-hole-style DNS ad blocking on an ESP32-C3 board, which its README puts at about US$2, under the MIT licence. The project was still being updated as of 6 October, and the README says lookups for blocklisted domains are answered with 0.0.0.0 while others are forwarded to an upstream DNS server. You point a device's DNS at the board, and the README's install steps involve compiling and flashing it yourself.

The README warns that leaving the default passwords in place makes the dashboard password effectively public, and that the dashboard runs over plain HTTP. Our reading of the main branch code on 12 October is that by default it forwards queries unencrypted to the public DNS service Quad9.

Mobile internet shutdown and a platform advisory in New Delhi

According to the Deccan Herald, India's Ministry of Home Affairs authorised a suspension of mobile internet services, covering all mobile technologies, within a 4 km radius of the Janpath–Kartavya Path crossing in New Delhi. The authorised window was 22:00 India time on 9 October to 22:00 on 10 October, coinciding with a protest. MediaNama reported that the order was marked top secret and did not state its grounds, and as of its 12 October update the ministry had not officially published it.

According to the full text published by MediaNama, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory on 8 October advising social media platforms to exercise enhanced diligence over false and misleading content that could affect public order and to prioritise reports from authorised government agencies. As of 12 October, the advisory was not on the ministry's website.

The digital rights group SFLC.IN argues that the shutdown was disproportionate and that not publishing the order beforehand breached the publication requirement in the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024. SFLC.IN also argues that the advisory's broad, vague wording could push platforms to over-remove lawful speech to protect their safe-harbour status.

Psiphon and Canada's Bill C-22

The Globe and Mail reported on 4 October that Psiphon, a Toronto company that helps users get around online censorship, told the paper it has started planning to move its operations out of Canada if the lawful access bill C-22 (Lawful Access Act, 2026) passes as written. The Citizen Lab's page says the bill would require electronic service providers to make secret changes to their systems to give police and intelligence services surveillance capabilities. A Psiphon vice-president wrote in an email reply to the paper that a secret backdoor cannot be built into open-source code because every line is public. As of 12 October, Psiphon's own website had no separate announcement.

In the same report, a spokesperson for the public safety minister said a lawful access framework does not, on its own, make it impossible to operate a secure, privacy-protective service in Canada. The report also notes that the House of Commons amended the bill before the summer recess, including an amendment protecting end-to-end encryption. As of 12 October, Parliament's LEGISinfo shows the bill at second reading in the Senate.

item.title: Compositor, an open-source image editor, and maintaining and auditing AI-generated code
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: A designer released Compositor, a free, open-source image editor for the Mac that needs no account, and says AI wrote all of its code. The criticism we found centers on the phrase "I built" and on who reviews and maintains AI-written code. As of 12 October it runs only on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 26 or later.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including Compositor, GitHub, X

A designer released Compositor, an image editor for the Mac, on GitHub on 16 September (UTC) and introduced it on X on 18 September. It is open source under the MIT license, free to download and needs no account, and the developer's launch post says it started as a tool for his own use, to get off an Adobe subscription. As of 12 October the latest release is 1.4.10 from 11 October (UTC), it runs only on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 26 or later, and the interface is English only, with translations not being accepted for now.

The launch post had about 2.4 million views by 12 October, but we could not retrieve the replies under it, so what follows draws only on a small number of public posts on X. A concept artist quoted the launch post to criticize calling AI-written software "I built", describing such work as vibe coding, meaning having AI write code from natural-language instructions. Replying to that post, the developer wrote "AI wrote every line of this" and "Code was always the painful part, never the important part." By our count of the GitHub commit history (the record of each change to the code) on 12 October, 282 of 451 commits carry a co-author credit for an AI coding tool.

A developer who builds creative tools, using the project to explore how AI will change the business of creative tools, wrote on X that its code is "decidedly not for human consumption", and asked what would keep the developer maintaining it over the next six months or two years. The developer replied that he will keep maintaining it because he uses it every day. He maintains only the Mac version and wrote on X that he has not tested any of the Windows or Linux ports others have made.

Perspective

On GitHub the developer describes Compositor as "a local, single-user editor with no network path". The release notes separately say it checks for updates at most once a day when opened, and updates wait for the user to install them. Reading the app's configuration, we confirmed that the update feed it checks is hosted on GitHub. On X the developer also wrote "no login, no account, no tracking".

An outside contributor submitted a pull request (a proposed code change) adding generative fill, which would send images out only if the user turned it on, supplied their own key for Google's Gemini AI service and pressed generate. The pull request itself says this would be the first feature to send user content off the Mac. The developer commented that he wanted to think about how AI should fit into Compositor long term, and the pull request was later closed without being merged. On a separate on-device AI upscaling feature, he wrote that he would rather rethink AI features as a whole, possibly in a v2.

Being open source means these claims can be checked rather than taken on trust. On 12 October we searched the main branch for keywords and found no network requests or analytics code apart from the update check, which is not a full audit. By our count the app has about 37,000 lines of Swift, most of it AI-generated judging by the commit credits. The creative-tools developer's description of that code is "decidedly not for human consumption".

On 19 September an outside contributor opened eight patch pull requests based on a security scan, one of which said crafted project values outside the expected range could make the inspector or adjustment editor stop working. The developer closed them as a batch, writing that the app is used locally by one person with no untrusted input, so these were "robustness questions rather than security ones". His comment does not say whether opening a project file someone else sent you counts as untrusted input.

His closing comment also explains that import, resizing and export are already capped at 100 megapixels and 30,000 pixels per side, and that the added limits risked refusing valid documents. It adds that the pull requests revealed the automated tests had not run for a while, and that after the fix there are 362 tests. He asked anyone who had actually reproduced a crash to open an issue (a problem report on the project) with the file and steps.

The developer says he will keep maintaining a tool he uses himself, and that people who want other platforms can port it under the MIT license, as other developers have done for Windows and other platforms. The creative-tools developer questions whether the author will keep maintaining features users ask for but he does not use himself, adding that software for ordinary users doesn't seem to have the consulting income, from services sold to companies, that supports many open-source projects. The contributor behind a separate Simplified Chinese fork (an independently modified copy) wrote in an issue on the original project that the fork removed automatic updates, so users are not updated back to the English build and do not hit the original update feed.

Anyone with an Apple silicon Mac on macOS 26 or later can try it from GitHub or Homebrew. Downloading requires no sign-up, though reporting problems requires a GitHub account. Based on the developer's statements and our keyword search, editing images involves no network access apart from the update check, which is on by default and leaves installation to the user. We have not fully audited the code, and the developer has not said whether opening project files from others carries any risk.

The official download and update feed are hosted on GitHub, which may matter to readers in mainland China. As of its last tests on 11 and 8 October, GreatFire reports interference in 64% of 56 conclusive tests of github.com over the past 90 days, and in all of its last 4 tests of raw.githubusercontent.com, where the update feed is hosted, a small sample. These are third-party measurements of host names, not of the specific download paths. The interface is English only, and the one Simplified Chinese fork we found is maintained by an outside contributor; we found no Taiwanese news coverage of Compositor and no source linking it to any regulation in Asia.

When comparing tools like this, a few questions apply. The developer values running locally, no login and freedom to modify the code, and those claims can be checked against the source and actual network connections. The critics care about maintenance and what happens to a feature you rely on if a sole maintainer stops updating it. Whether anyone has read the AI-written code, and how outside reports are handled, can also be seen in a project's issues and pull requests.

item.title: Country-code top-level domain hijacks and unauthorized HTTPS certificates
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Google announced on 6 October that the .gh, .sl and .as country-code top-level domains were hijacked and attackers obtained HTTPS certificates for Google and other organizations. Chrome has blocked the certificates it found; domain owners can monitor Certificate Transparency logs.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 15 sources, including Google, Let's Encrypt Community Forum, Ars Technica

Google announced on 6 October that the .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone) and .as (American Samoa) country-code top-level domains (ccTLDs) had been hijacked, and that attackers used this to obtain HTTPS certificates for several Google domains and for domains of other organizations. The announcement says the domains at risk are those ending in these three codes, and that Google's own systems were not compromised. Chrome has blocked the certificates Google found, and the announcement says Chrome users do not need to take any action.

According to Google, the attackers compromised these three third-party-operated ccTLDs and modified authoritative DNS records, the records that say where a domain points. The announcement does not say where the attackers got in, for example the operator's systems or a registrar account, or when the hijacks began, and as of 12 October we, a community based in Taiwan, could not find any statement from the three operators. Ars Technica reports that control of the DNS records let the attackers pass certificate authorities' domain control validation (DCV), the check that an applicant really controls a domain, while iThome writes that they may have passed it this way. Google writes that it has no reason to believe the issuing certificate authorities did anything wrong.

Google first blocked the certificates for its own domains through CRLSets, Chrome's emergency certificate blocklist, and asked the issuing CAs to revoke them. Certificate Transparency (CT) logs, public logs that record every issued certificate, then revealed other organizations believed to be affected by the same attacks, including leading global brands and widely used online services, and Chrome blocked those certificates as well. A Let's Encrypt staff member confirmed on its forum that it had issued certificates for Google and YouTube and that they have been revoked. iTnews compared CT logs against Chrome's blocklist and found 32 certificates issued to the attackers between 22 and 27 September, a count CircleID notes has not been independently reproduced.

Perspective

An HTTPS certificate vouches that a site is the one it claims to be. Before issuing one, a certificate authority checks that the applicant controls the domain, and one way is to ask the applicant to publish a specific DNS record. DNS is delegated downward from the top-level domain, so we infer that when the layer above is hijacked, an attacker can pass validation even though the owner of the domain below did nothing wrong. Google's announcement notes that CAs may reuse earlier validation results, and lists shorter certificate lifetimes and shorter validation reuse periods among its long-term improvements.

The other possibly affected organizations were found by Google in Certificate Transparency logs. Chrome and Safari require publicly trusted certificates to be recorded in public logs that anyone can search. The certificates Google found were all found in those logs. Our reading is that CT lets such certificates be discovered after issuance and does not stop them at the moment of issuance.

Google also writes that Chrome's blocking does not reliably protect users of other browsers, and that it cannot guarantee it identified every affected domain. The announcement says the certificates for Google domains were revoked with the CAs' help, but for other organizations it only says Chrome blocked them, while iTnews reports that the CAs have revoked the bogus certificates it found. Privacy Guides writes that Firefox handles them with CRLite, its revocation checking mechanism, and as of 12 October we found nothing from Safari or Edge. CircleID notes that, as of 8 October, how much traffic may have been intercepted had not been established publicly.

Google recommends that domain owners continuously monitor CT logs for all of their domains, including parked and regional ccTLD domains, and that anyone with a .gh, .sl or .as domain review recent entries for unexpected certificates. Services such as Cloudflare and Cert Spotter send alerts when a new certificate is issued. Cloudflare's alerts are switched on from its Edge Certificates page and are off by default, and Cert Spotter's site lists a 30-day free trial. Google also recommends CAA records, which name the CAs allowed to issue for a domain, ideally bound to specific ACME accounts (ACME being the protocol Let's Encrypt and others use for automated issuance).

Google writes that CAA cannot prevent issuance during an active DNS hijack. Its value comes after DNS control is restored, when it stops an attacker from using earlier validation results to obtain new certificates. CT monitoring likewise helps owners find out sooner after the fact, and Google's recommendations include nothing a domain owner can do to block this kind of upstream hijack in advance.

Several registries in Asia offer registry-level locks, which add update, transfer and delete prohibitions to a domain. In Taiwan, TWNIC's Registry Lock lists NT$6,000 per domain per year, with a NT$4,800 first-year price for new applications until 31 December 2026, as of 12 October. Japan's JPRS offers its registry lock only through designated registrars, whose offerings vary. Hong Kong's HKIRC announced .hk LOCK in 2014, with each change verified by human contact, and we could not confirm its current terms.

These locks guard against unauthorized changes to registration data, and TWNIC writes that its lock still protects a domain even if the registrar is compromised. We found no official description of a registry lock from South Korea's KRNIC. We found no official statement on whether a lock helps when the registry operator itself is breached, and Google's recommendations do not mention locks.

As of 12 October, we found no disclosure from the three operators, the issuing CAs or the Asian registries above about how the attackers got in, and no full list of the certificates. It is worth checking again in mid-November for any incident report that explains the point of entry.

item.title: BentoPDF, an open-source toolkit for processing PDFs locally in the browser
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to its developers, the open-source BentoPDF toolkit merges, compresses, OCRs and strips metadata from PDFs inside the browser, without uploading files to an online converter. It works straight from its website, and some features download code from the third-party jsDelivr service when used.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 15 sources, including BentoPDF, GitHub, It's FOSS

It's FOSS introduced the open-source PDF toolkit BentoPDF on 10 October; its website lists more than 100 tools. According to its developers, merging, splitting, compressing, OCR (optical character recognition, which turns scanned images into searchable text), encryption and metadata removal all happen in the browser, with no upload to a server. It works straight from the website without sign-up, and the interface is available in Traditional and Simplified Chinese. As of 12 October the latest release is 2.8.8, published on 29 August.

The project's privacy policy says processing is done by JavaScript and WebAssembly libraries running on the user's device and that files are not uploaded, and that the site uses no cookies or analytics. Components such as PyMuPDF, used for compression and PDF-to-Word conversion, are not part of BentoPDF's own source code; the README says the browser downloads them from jsDelivr, a third-party service that distributes code files for websites, when they are used. The OCR page likewise says the OCR engine and selected language packs are downloaded on first use, while the scanned pages and recognized text stay on the device.

The code is published on GitHub under AGPL-3.0, with a separate one-time US$79 commercial license for closed-source products. The project was started by a single developer, and its about page says more than 60 people have since contributed code, translations and fixes. People who would rather not use the website can run it on their own computer or server with Docker, which packages the whole program into a ready-to-run bundle.

Perspective

Online converters send files to their own servers and back, and how long they keep the files depends on each service's policy. iLovePDF's privacy policy says files are deleted within two hours of processing, except for its e-signature service. Smallpdf's privacy notice says it generally aims to delete files from users who are not logged in "within a reasonable period of time" after they were last opened, with each reopening extending that period, while its blog says files from free use are deleted after one hour. The Taipei City Government's Department of Information Technology also told its staff in 2023 to avoid online conversion and encryption services, because there is no way to be sure how such services store and use the data they receive.

BentoPDF's privacy policy says local processing avoids exposure in transit and on a server. Our inference is that trust shifts to the code on the web page instead. When using the official site, you run whatever version the site serves at that moment, and updates do not require the user's consent. Advanced features also load code from jsDelivr, and the official FAQ separately says a few tools that need external data may need a connection.

One of the security advisories the project has published on GitHub describes how importing a crafted workflow file can send the PDF's SHA-256 hash (a digest calculated from the file's contents, not the file itself) to an attacker's server. The advisory lists 2.8.6 and earlier as affected, and as of 12 October it lists no patched version.

Even when processed locally, a PDF can still carry hidden properties such as its author and creation time. BentoPDF's metadata removal tool clears them, and its "Sanitize PDF" tool also removes annotations and scripts, which is worth doing before sharing a file.

Anyone who needs to merge or convert documents containing personal data without uploading them to an online service can use the website directly, and every tool is free. The official FAQ says there is no file size limit beyond what your own computer can handle.

Those who want to pin a version can self-host with Docker as described in the README, which requires installing Docker and using the command line. Networks with no internet access need the README's separate offline deployment steps, packaging the required components on a connected machine first. The privacy policy also says the safety of files depends on your own computer and browser. Our inference is that local processing offers no protection if the computer itself is compromised.

Official cautions about online services in Asia that we found are addressed to public servants. Besides Taipei's notice to city staff, mainland China's Ministry of State Security warned in August 2024 that staff in classified positions must not upload classified documents to the internet or feed them into text recognition features, listing format conversion among the functions of online office platforms; it does not address ordinary users or PDF converters. Japan's 2023 guidance on generative AI from the executive committee (kanjikai) of the Digital Society Promotion Council says government bodies cannot handle confidential information in cloud services that are used just by accepting standard terms, but it does not name file converters. We, a community based in Taiwan, did not find a notice about online converters from Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs or the Executive Yuan, and could not retrieve an official South Korean text, only press coverage of a generative AI guideline.

item.title: Let's Encrypt's 64-day default certificate lifetime
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Let's Encrypt will cut its default certificate lifetime from 90 to 64 days from 10 February 2027. Anyone running a site or self-hosted service on its certificates should check that automatic renewal is not tied to a fixed number of days. The announcement says nothing to ordinary visitors.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including Let's Encrypt, CA/Browser Forum, Ars Technica

Let's Encrypt announced on 7 October that certificates issued or renewed from 10 February 2027 will have a default lifetime of 64 days instead of 90. The last 90-day certificates are expected to expire on 11 May 2027, and valid certificates will not be revoked. The announcement only asks things of people running sites and self-hosted services, and says nothing to ordinary visitors.

The staging environment switches to 64-day certificates on 14 October, and Let's Encrypt recommends testing there first. Under its December 2025 announcement, the default drops again to 45 days on 16 February 2028, and anyone who wants to move early can already choose a 45-day or 6-day profile (a named set of certificate settings requested at issuance).

Let's Encrypt says shorter lifetimes reduce the risk of key compromise and mis-issuance. A ballot passed in April 2025 by the CA/Browser Forum, where certificate authorities and browser makers set the rules for certificates, cuts the maximum lifetime from 398 days in steps: 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029. Since 64 days is shorter than the 2027 cap, our reading of the two announcements is that it is an intermediate step Let's Encrypt chose before the 47-day limit arrives.

Perspective

A certificate proves that a site is who it claims to be, and a leaked key or mis-issued certificate can be used to impersonate the site until it expires. Shorter lifetimes shrink that window, which, according to Let's Encrypt's 2015 explanation, was one of its reasons for choosing 90 days. The cost is more frequent renewal: a February post expects daily renewal requests to double once lifetimes reach 45 days. The December 2025 announcement advises against manual renewal, and rate limits are not affected.

The software that requests and renews certificates is called an ACME client, such as Certbot. If renewal is automated and the client supports ARI (ACME Renewal Information, which lets the certificate authority tell the client when to renew, published as RFC 9773 in 2025), the announcement says no change is needed, and Certbot has checked ARI by default since version 4.1.0 in June 2025. Let's Encrypt recommends that anyone who hard-coded renewal at a fixed number of days switch to renewing at about two-thirds of the lifetime, and suggests searching cron jobs, scripts and runbooks for numbers such as 83, 80 or 60 if unsure.

Certificate authorities in Asia have announced their own changes for the CA/Browser Forum caps, and the three announcements we read do not mention Let's Encrypt's 64 days. Taiwan Certificate Authority (TWCA) set a 198-day lifetime from 9 March 2026, meaning two applications a year, and Japan Registry Services (JPRS) cut its server certificates from one year to five months from 18 February 2026 while leaving its ACME-based service unchanged. In South Korea, Korea Information Certificate Authority (KICA), which sells Sectigo certificates, published the CA/Browser Forum schedule in April 2025. TWCA and JPRS were among the five certificate issuers that abstained in the 2025 ballot.

Site operators using Let's Encrypt can check now whether their client supports ARI, run a renewal against staging after 14 October and, as the announcement suggests, add alerts for failed renewals. The announcement says nothing specific about devices that only accept certificates uploaded through a web interface. By our count, using each certificate for the full 64 days still means six replacements a year, or about nine if renewed at two-thirds as recommended, and Let's Encrypt's client list explains that it leaves out in-browser ACME clients because they encourage manual renewal, which increases the risk of missed renewals.

item.title: Apple's planned changes to granting Full Disk Access on the Mac
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Apple said on 2 October that it will require very explicit user action before a Mac app can be granted Full Disk Access, citing some developers' use of the permission and the growing risk from AI agents. Apple gave no version or date, and as of 12 October its release notes do not mention the control.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including Apple, TechCrunch, Decrypt

Apple said in a developer news post on 2 October that it will add controls to macOS Full Disk Access so that users who genuinely want to grant it can only do so with very explicit user action. Apple did not say which version, when, what the interface will look like, or whether apps already granted access will need confirming again. As of 12 October, neither the macOS 27 nor the macOS 27.2 beta 3 release notes mention the new control.

Apple's post says Full Disk Access largely sidesteps the controls that protect user data so that backup apps can work on the Mac. It also says some developers use it in ways that could expose files, mail, messages and even browsing history without users' full knowledge, and that the risk will grow substantially as AI agents (AI programs that can operate a computer and read files and apps on a user's behalf) become more capable and autonomous. TechCrunch later corrected its report, which had described the change as Apple "limiting" permissions, to say it is about informed consent and is not a new limit.

A few days earlier, according to TechCrunch and Decrypt, a columnist said Meta's AI agent Muse for Mac had read his private messages while Full Disk Access was off (our 9 October post covered this). According to Decrypt, he had declined Messages access during setup and later found Muse had synced the Mac's local Messages database. Meta's VP of Communications said on X on 30 September that Muse can only read Messages if both Full Disk Access and Muse's own Messages connector are enabled. Apple's post names no app or developer, and it was Ars Technica and iThome that framed the two as contradicting each other.

Perspective

Full Disk Access is an operating-system permission, and Apple's support page says it lets an app access all files on the computer, including data from other apps such as Mail and Messages and Time Machine backups. A macOS security expert quoted by Ars Technica said a program with this permission can read files such as browsing history, browser cookies and chats. A Meta executive said, as relayed by TechCrunch, that reading Messages goes through in-app permissions and macOS system-level protections that cannot be bypassed even if the app had a bug. Apple's support page and the security expert describe what an app can read once it has the permission, while Meta's statements describe which authorisation steps Muse requires.

Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), released by Microsoft on 7 October, takes a different approach. According to Microsoft's post, developers or IT administrators write a policy defining which files and network destinations an AI agent can use, and the policy sits outside the agent's control. MXC is open source under the MIT licence and uses the macOS Seatbelt sandbox (a mechanism that limits which resources a program can reach). Its README says it is an SDK built into apps, and Microsoft's list of supported tools includes GitHub Copilot and OpenAI Codex but not Muse or ChatGPT, so in our reading ordinary users will not configure it directly.

Neither Microsoft's nor Apple's documents mention the other, and it is our choice to set them side by side. The difference is who acts as the gatekeeper: Apple's plan makes users more aware of what they are granting at the moment of consent, while MXC lets developers limit in advance what an agent can touch. Apple's post does not say whether the new control will change what Full Disk Access can read. Things to watch are when the control appears in macOS release notes and whether existing grants need reconfirming.

We compared South Korea, Japan and Taiwan on one question: is there a rule requiring operating-system or app makers to provide ways to grant and withdraw access permissions? South Korea has one. Article 22-2(3) of its Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection (the version in force from 2 October 2026, checked on 12 October) requires mobile operating-system makers, device makers and software suppliers to take measures such as providing ways for users to consent to and withdraw app access permissions, though it covers mobile devices and is not aimed at AI agents. What we found for Japan is a June 2023 warning from the Personal Information Protection Commission to users about entering personal data into generative AI services (we did not check for later updates), and for Taiwan, the AI Basic Act of January 2026, which places privacy-by-design duties on government agencies rather than on app or operating-system makers.

Mac users can open System Settings, then Privacy & Security, then Full Disk Access to see which apps have it. For an unfamiliar app, it is worth finding out why it needs the permission, bearing in mind that backup apps are the use Apple's post names. Apple's support page only describes adding apps, while Meta says Muse's access can be revoked at any time. Before granting it, remember that it lets an app read messages other people have sent you and your browsing history, a judgement that will still be yours to make after Apple's new control arrives.

item.title: Brave's Email Aliases
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Brave's desktop browser offers email aliases from version 1.94, letting you sign up with a forwarding address instead of your real one. Everyone gets five free, with a Brave account required. As of 12 October there is no mobile version, and Brave does not say whether you can reply from an alias.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 14 sources, including Brave, GitHub, Apple

Brave launched Email Aliases on 27 August. From desktop version 1.94, you can sign up for websites with a forwarding address instead of your real email. Everyone gets five for free, but you first need a Brave account, which is separate from the Premium account used for services such as Brave VPN. As of 12 October, the Android and iOS release notes do not include the feature, and the help page exists only in English and Japanese.

A prompt to create an alias appears in a site's email field, and if it does not, you can right-click the field and choose "New Email Alias". Brave's announcement and privacy policy say Brave does not read the emails and only performs standard spam and virus filtering. Messages are deleted within seconds of delivery, failed deliveries are retried for up to 24 hours, and the forwarding runs on Amazon Web Services. The announcement also warns that some forwarded mail may land in spam at first.

The Brave account launched the same day signs in with OPAQUE, a protocol that lets a server verify a user without holding the password, published as RFC 9807 in July 2025. Brave's post says the password itself is never sent to its servers. The same post says OPAQUE does not stop phishing on its own and does not make weak passwords strong.

Perspective

Brave's announcement calls an email address a durable, universal identifier and cites ad tools from Meta, Google and LinkedIn that let advertisers upload customer emails to match users. That matching happens between servers, so tracker blocking in the browser cannot stop it. With a different alias for each site, sites cannot use your email to match you across them.

The announcement says Brave stores the account email and every alias, encrypted at rest, so the link between aliases and the real address sits on Brave's servers. The help page says Brave logs receipt times and some headers for debugging but not message content or sender information, and the privacy policy says these logs are deleted within 14 days at most. The policy also says Brave will not reveal the emails or aliases tied to an account unless obliged by a valid legal request. Brave's pages do not say whether you can reply from an alias or which domain the aliases use.

An open-source list that sites use to block disposable email added bravealias.com, reported in an issue as Brave's alias domain, to its stricter tier in September. The maintainer noted that it is a forwarding relay rather than disposable mail, that it belongs in the same category as Firefox Relay and SimpleLogin, which is why it went only into the stricter tier, and only sites that use that tier block such domains.

Apple's Hide My Email comes with a paid iCloud+ plan and supports replies. Firefox Relay gives five free masks, with anonymous replies on the paid plan, whose list of countries does not include Taiwan or Hong Kong. SimpleLogin is open source, and its free plan offers ten aliases with replies.

In Hong Kong, Taiwan and mainland China, aliases do nothing for sites that ask for a phone number at sign-up, because a phone number there is tied to a real name. As of 12 October we found no rules in these places aimed specifically at email aliases or forwarding addresses.

Under Hong Kong's Telecommunications (Registration of SIM Cards) Regulation, all SIM cards have had to be registered under a real name since 2022. Article 77 of Taiwan's Regulations Governing Mobile Broadband Services (in the version we checked) requires carriers to record subscribers' names, addresses and two ID numbers before activation, prepaid cards included. Mainland China's Cybersecurity Law, amended in October 2025, requires operators of services including messaging and posting to collect users' real identity information.

Desktop Brave users on 1.94 or later can type brave://settings/email-aliases into the address bar, create an account and start generating aliases. Brave's source code already includes a Traditional Chinese translation of the setting. An alias protects only the email address, so sites can still match you through a phone number, real name or payment details used at sign-up.

item.title: The Tor Project's decision on its relationship with Mullvad, and the debate around it
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: After a political donation by a co-founder of VPN provider Mullvad drew criticism, the Tor Project said on 9 October that it would keep working with Mullvad but pause co-branding and revise how it describes Mullvad Browser. Neither browser has announced a halt in maintenance, and comments on the statement are divided.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including Tor Project, Tor Project Forum, Mullvad

After a political donation by a co-founder of VPN provider Mullvad drew criticism, the Tor Project published a statement on 9 October saying it would not end its relationship with Mullvad. The statement says it is setting clear boundaries: technical collaboration continues under the two parties' narrowly scoped agreement, proactive co-branding is paused, and Tor has revised how its own channels describe Mullvad Browser. As of 12 October, the latest stable release of both Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser is 15.0.24 from late September, and neither has announced a halt in maintenance.

The controversy began with a 26 June report by Swedish outlet Flamman: in 2025 one co-founder personally gave 5 million Swedish kronor to the Swedish party Örebropartiet, 72% of the party's income that year. Flamman calls it a populist party that advocates large-scale remigration. In a 20 July blog post, Mullvad said it was a private donation the company was not involved in, that it "does not condone it, nor condemn it", and that it "most likely was a bad idea".

Tor's statement says the collaboration improved the structure, maintainability and auditability of Tor Browser's code and gave more people another free, open-source privacy tool. Tor's IRS Form 990 for July 2023 to June 2024 lists about US$1.4 million from Mullvad, the largest corporate source. The statement gives no figures, and as of 12 October Tor's financials page only goes up to the year ending June 2024.

Perspective

Mullvad Browser launched in April 2023 and is distributed by Mullvad; Tor describes it as "Tor Browser without the Tor Network". The two share version numbers and release dates, and Mullvad Browser is signed by the Tor Browser developers, so in our reading they share most of their code. The difference is the connection: Tor Browser uses the Tor network, reaches onion services and has built-in censorship circumvention, while Mullvad Browser is meant to be used with a VPN the user trusts, or without one.

Tor's statement says it defends free speech but strongly opposes rhetoric that threatens other human rights and freedoms, and that privacy work is severely under-resourced and sometimes requires difficult compromises. Mullvad's post says the company stands for freedom of speech, freedom of information and privacy, and keeps its mission separate from its founders' personal views. A volunteer group that runs one Snowflake bridge (an entry point to Tor for people on censored networks), and says it is not part of the Tor Project, announced on 5 August that it would refuse Mullvad's donations because they went to what it called a "dangerous populist political party", even though that leaves only about a quarter of what it needs to cover annual expenses.

The forum comments under Tor's blog post numbered eight as of 12 October, three supporting the continued relationship and three critical or condemning (comments are a small, self-selected group and do not represent the community as a whole). Supporters wrote that Mullvad's mission aligns with Tor's and that losing Mullvad Browser would harm users.

On the critical side, one comment condemned the decision outright. Another, from someone who says they are a former Tor Browser developer, wrote that Mullvad has no developers on the browser and only provides money, so calling it "technical collaboration" is misleading. Tor's support page says the browser is developed by the Tor Project in collaboration with Mullvad, and Mullvad's announcement says Tor's engineers develop it; neither says whether Mullvad staff take part.

Tor's statement says the decision followed discussions with the community, staff and board, a staff survey and financial analysis, but it has not published the survey results or the figures. One forum comment asked what share of the budget comes from Mullvad and whether all donations get the same scrutiny. As of 12 October, no Tor Project staff had replied in the thread, and Mullvad's blog had no new post about the statement.

On Hacker News, the thread about the statement had 353 comments by 12 October, with 22 visible top-level comments (another 11 were flagged and hidden), which are likewise not representative. Four top-level comments understood or supported the decision, two of them arguing that funding for such tools is scarce and cutting ties may not serve the mission better. Five disputed the line the statement draws on speech, for example arguing that free speech is absolute, while replies countered that Tor simply does not want to be associated with that speech. Three criticised the statement for leaving out the details of the donation and party or for sounding like corporate PR, and one worried that relying on Mullvad's money could affect Tor's independence.

As of 12 October, GreatFire's third-party monitoring showed mullvad.net failing its last 16 conclusive tests in mainland China, and www.torproject.org failing both of its only two conclusive tests, the latest about two months earlier. In our reading, getting either browser in mainland China means getting around the block first, and Tor's decision does not change that.

Readers using Tor Browser or Mullvad Browser do not need to change anything as of 12 October. The dispute is about funding and organisational positions, and in our reading, given that the technical collaboration continues under the agreement, the browsers' privacy protections are unaffected. Readers who mind the funding should note that Tor Project engineers maintain both browsers, so switching from one to the other does not change the money flowing between Tor and Mullvad. Things to watch are whether the co-branding pause has an end date, whether Tor discloses Mullvad's recent share of its funding, and the next financial report.

Questions for comparison: what standard should a privacy-tool developer use to vet corporate funders, and is it applied consistently; can a company be judged separately from a founder's personal political donation; do pausing promotion and revising descriptions let users tell the scope of a collaboration from an organisation's position; and could an open-source browser still in maintenance find other funding if the collaboration ended?

item.title: Firefox for iOS's built-in ad blocker and system-level blocking on Android
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Firefox on iPhone and iPad now has a built-in ad blocker, first listed in the 156 release notes in mid-September. It is off by default. On Android, the system-level options surveyed in a personal blog post mostly mean trusting whoever runs the service or app.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 9 sources, including Mozilla, Kevin Boone, Google

Mozilla announced on 1 September that Firefox on iPhone and iPad now includes a built-in ad blocker. It is off by default and can be turned on under Settings > Browsing. The feature first appeared in the release notes for version 156, published on 15 September, and Mozilla was quoted as saying it is being rolled out gradually. Desktop and Android versions of Firefox could already install ad-blocking extensions, so the change only affects iOS.

The announcement says the blocker uses Apple's WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter list to stop many third-party ads and ad-related trackers before they load. Mozilla says extensions work differently on iOS, so it built the feature into the browser, and that it made the feature optional because advertising funds much of the web. Ads served directly by the site, ads in search results and sponsored shortcuts on Firefox's new tab page are not affected.

For blocking ads across a whole Android phone, a personal blog post published on 1 October surveys four approaches for 2026: an ad-blocking DNS service (DNS turns domain names into IP addresses), a VPN service with ad blocking, a local VPN app that does not need root, and editing the system hosts file with root access. As far as the author knows, all of them work by overriding DNS, mapping known advertisers' hostnames to bogus IP addresses.

Perspective

Both approaches block known ad addresses before a connection is made, but at different scopes. Firefox's blocker on iOS applies only to pages opened in Firefox, using WebKit's content blocking, and Apple's App Review Guidelines require apps that browse the web to use WebKit, with separate exemption procedures for the EU and Japan. Android's system-level methods cover every app, although, as the author notes, they cannot stop ads built into an app or apps that connect by IP address (which the author says is still rare).

In our reading, the first three methods mean trusting whoever provides the service, since every domain your apps look up passes through it. The author warns that a rogue DNS or VPN operator could even redirect online banking to its own proxy, and suggests that people who care about privacy pick a no-logs provider that supports encrypted DNS. Local VPN apps route all traffic through a single app, so the author advises using only open-source ones. The root method avoids an outside operator, at the cost of checking what gets written to the hosts file.

Apple's guidelines name only the EU and Japan as places where browsers may use engines other than WebKit, with Japan included from iOS 26.2, though Firefox's ad blocker is built on WebKit's content blocking either way. Firefox's source code includes Japanese, Korean and Traditional Chinese strings for the blocker, so the setting is localised in all three markets alike. On Android, Google's developer verification began on 30 September for apps installed from participating stores, with the page listing only Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand so far and a global rollout planned for 2027. That matters for the local VPN apps the author says are hard to get through Google Play, though the page names no such apps.

iPhone and iPad users who update Firefox to the latest version, which needs iOS 15.0 or later, should find the switch under Settings > Browsing. The interface text suggests turning it off if a site breaks, and site-served ads, search ads and new tab sponsored content will still appear. On Android, the author suggests that if web ads are the main problem, the simplest approach might be a browser with ad blocking. To block ads in apps too, enter an ad-blocking DNS provider's hostname under Settings > Network & internet > Private DNS (menus vary by manufacturer; prices vary and most offer a free trial), after checking its logging policy, since every app's lookups will go to that provider.

item.title: Beeline's AI voice personas for scam calls
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Russian carrier Beeline said on 6 October that it has routed 19.1 million scam calls to AI voice personas since the start of 2026, according to its own figures. The service runs only on Beeline's network in Russia. In South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, the examples we found are call warnings, filtering and on-device detection.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including Beeline, ict-online, 動區動趨

Russian mobile carrier Beeline said on 6 October that its anti-fraud platform has routed 19.1 million scam calls to a set of AI voice personas since the start of 2026. Beeline calls them its "cyber family", and according to the press release, scammers have spent about 140,000 hours talking to them, close to 6,000 days. The service runs only on Beeline's network in Russia, and all figures are self-reported without independent verification.

Beeline began small-scale tests of a "cyber granny" in November 2025 with a single voice, and the release at the time said suspicious calls to older female customers would be routed to it. The system analyses what the scammer says, then a large language model generates a reply from the conversation's context and turns it into speech. A teenage persona was added in June 2026, and in August Beeline announced ten voices in total, with almost all scam calls on its network now sent to them. The AI picks a voice based on the number being called, and a scammer who calls the same number again within five hours reaches the same persona.

Beeline's June 2026 release says the service is part of the free basic tier of its "My Security" (Моя безопасность) service. The chief executive said on 6 October that these calls are also a large body of material for retraining the models. The releases do not say whether the protected customer's phone rings, whether customers can switch the service off, or what happens when a real person's call is misrouted to the AI.

Perspective

According to Beeline's releases, its anti-fraud platform decides which calls look suspicious and where to send them, without publishing the criteria. The point of stalling scammers is to use up their time so they make fewer calls to real people. O2 in the UK launched a similar AI granny, Daisy, in November 2024, and its press release says Daisy kept scammers on the line for up to 40 minutes at a time, without saying how many calls it took.

Both the decision and the routing happen on the carrier's side, and as of 12 October Beeline has not published how misrouted calls are handled. The releases say the calls are used for retraining but not whether recordings or transcripts are kept, for how long, or on what legal basis. South Korea offers a contrast. According to the government's policy news site, the Ministry of Science and ICT said in July 2025 that a scammer's voice counts as sensitive information under Korea's Personal Information Protection Act, so the carrier KT needed a regulatory sandbox exemption (a trial scheme that temporarily exempts a limited use from existing rules) to use such voice data without consent for an AI service that detects scams during calls.

In the three places we checked, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, we found no carrier offering AI personas that answer scam calls as of 12 October, only call warnings, filtering and on-device detection. In February 2026 Korea's science ministry urged people to use AI scam-call detection from Samsung and the three mobile carriers, noting that call analysis runs on the phone itself rather than on outside servers. Singapore's ScamShield combines an app that helps people check, block and filter scams with a 24/7 helpline at 1799. In Taiwan, Chunghwa Telecom introduced a spoken warning in July 2023 for international calls showing a "+886 9" prefix on landlines.

Wherever you are, the advice from Taiwan's Criminal Investigation Bureau, relayed by the Ministry of the Interior, is to hang up first and then verify through an official channel. In Taiwan, a caller who asks you to dial 165, the anti-fraud hotline, without hanging up first is a scammer. The 165 hotline and the 165 website take enquiries and reports. Carrier-side call interception like Beeline's only handles incoming phone calls, so in our view scams that start in messaging apps still need checking yourself.
